# The Peculiar Joy of Getting Lost

I've been thinking about how getting lost has become almost impossible, and what we've lost because of it.

My parents have a story about taking a wrong turn on a family road trip in 1987, ending up in a small town two hours off their intended route. They spent the afternoon in a diner, talked to locals, discovered a waterfall hike, made memories that shaped their year. They laugh about it now.

Today, that wrong turn wouldn't happen. GPS would course-correct immediately, algorithmically efficient and utterly predictable.

There's something valuable in that old kind of lostness—the uncertainty that forces you to actually look around, to notice things. To talk to people. To be present in a place rather than just passing through it on your way to somewhere else.

I'm not romantic enough to think we should abandon navigation technology. But I wonder if we've optimized something important out of existence. The friction of not knowing exactly where you are creates space for discovery. It humbles you. It makes you pay attention.

I tried it intentionally last month—drove without GPS, just a vague idea of direction. Felt absurdly anxious for the first ten minutes, then something shifted. I noticed the quality of light on storefronts. A bookstore I'd never seen. Stopped for coffee and actually talked to the barista.

Maybe the solution isn't to abandon our tools, but to use them less reflexively. To occasionally choose the long way. To get deliberately lost, remembering that some of the best moments come when we don't know exactly where we're going.
